danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Samme aften, efter at have taget afsked med krigsministeren, begav Bolkonskij sig af sted for at slutte sig til hæren igen. Han vidste ikke, hvor han ville finde den, og frygtede at blive taget til fange af franskmændene undervejs til Krems.

I Brünn pakkede alle med tilknytning til hoffet sammen, og det tunge bagage var allerede blevet sendt til Olmütz. Nær Hetzelsdorf nåede fyrst Andrej hovedvejen, ad hvilken den russiske hær bevægede sig i stor hast og i den største uorden. Vejen var så tilstoppet af vogne, at det var umuligt at komme forbi i en karet. Fyrst Andrej skaffede sig en hest og en kosaksoldat fra en kosakkommandør og red sulten og udmattet forbi bagagevognene i sin søgen efter den øverstkommanderende og sit eget bagage. Meget ildevarslende rygter om hærens stilling nåede ham undervejs, og synet af tropperne i deres uordnede flugt bekræftede disse rygter.

»Cette armée russe que l'or de l'Angleterre a transportée des extrémités de l'univers, nous allons lui faire éprouver le même sort — (le sort de l'armée d'Ulm).« Han huskede disse ord fra Bonapartes tale til sin hær ved felttogets begyndelse, og de vakte i ham forundring over hans helts geni, en følelse af såret stolthed og et håb om berømmelse. »Og skulle der ikke være andet tilbage end at dø?« tænkte han. »Nå, om det skal være, vil jeg ikke gøre det ringere end andre.«
»Denne russiske hær, som Englands guld har bragt fra verdens ende, skal vi lade dele samme skæbne — (skæbnen over hæren ved Ulm).«

Han så med foragt på den endeløse, forvirrede masse af afdelinger, vogne, kanoner, artilleri og atter bagagevogne og køretøjer af enhver slags, der overhalede hinanden og blokerede den mudrede vej tre og undertiden fire i bredden. Fra alle sider, bagfra og forfra, så langt øret rakte, hørtes raslen af hjul, knirken fra vogne og kanonlavetter, tramp af heste, smæld af piske, råb, tilskyndelse af heste og soldaternes, ordonansernes og officerernes banden. Langs hele vejkanten lå faldne heste, nogle flåede, andre ikke, og ødelagte vogne, hvor ensomme soldater sad og ventede på noget, og atter soldater, der strejfede fra deres kompagnier — flokke af dem drog til de nærliggende landsbyer eller vendte tilbage med får, høns, hø og bugnende sække. Ved hver stigning og hver nedkørsel var trængslen endnu tættere og larmen af råb endnu mere uophørlig. Soldater, der vadede i mudder til knæene, skubbede selv kanoner og vogne frem. Piske smældede, hove gled, skagler gik i stykker, og lunger blev anspændt af råben. Officererne, der dirigerede marchen, red frem og tilbage mellem vognene. Deres stemmer var knap hørlige i larmen, og man kunne se på deres ansigter, at de havde opgivet håbet om at bringe orden i dette kaos.
»Her er vores kære ortodokse russiske hær,« tænkte Bolkonskij og mindedes Bilibins ord.

I ønsket om at finde ud af, hvor den øverstkommanderende var, red han hen til en konvoj. Lige over for ham kom et underligt etspænderkøretøj, åbenbart sammensat af soldater af hvad som helst tilgængeligt materiale og lignende noget midt imellem en kærre, en kabriolet og en kaleche. En soldat kørte, og en kvinde indhyllet i sjaler sad bag opslaget under vognens læderkaleche. Fyrst Andrej red derhen og var lige ved at stille sit spørgsmål til en soldat, da hans opmærksomhed blev afledt af kvindens desperate skrig fra vognen. En transportofficer slog den soldat, der kørte kvindens vogn, fordi han forsøgte at komme foran de andre, og piskeslagene faldt på vognens opslag. Kvinden skreg gennemtrængende. Da hun fik øje på fyrst Andrej, lænede hun sig ud bag opslaget og viftede med sine tynde arme under uldsjalet og råbte:

»Hr. adjutant! Hr. adjutant!... For Guds skyld... Beskyt mig! Hvad skal der blive af os? Jeg er kone til lægen ved det syvende jægerregiment... De lader os ikke passere, vi er blevet efterladt og har mistet vores folk...«
»Jeg skal banke dig flad som en pandekage!« råbte den vrede officer til soldaten. »Vend om med din tøjte!«
»Hr. adjutant! Hjælp mig!... Hvad skal alt dette betyde?« skreg lægekonen.
»Vær venlig at lade denne vogn passere. Kan De ikke se, det er en kvinde?« sagde fyrst Andrej, idet han red hen til officeren.
Officeren så på ham og vendte sig uden at svare atter mod soldaten. »Jeg skal lære dig at mase dig frem!... Tilbage!«
»Lad dem passere, siger jeg!« gentog fyrst Andrej og pressede læberne sammen.

»Og hvem er De?« råbte officeren og vendte sig mod ham i beruset raseri. »Hvem er De? Er det Dem, der fører kommandoen her? Hva'? Det er mig, der kommanderer her, ikke Dem! Tilbage, eller jeg banker Dem flad som en pandekage!« gentog han. Udtrykket behagede ham åbenbart.
»Det var en fin irettesættelse til den lille adjutant,« lød en stemme bagfra.

Fyrst Andrej så, at officeren var i den tilstand af sanseløs, drukken raseri, hvor et menneske ikke ved, hvad det siger. Han indså, at hans forsvar for lægekonen i hendes besynderlige farkost kunne udsætte ham for det, han frygtede mere end noget andet i verden — latterliggørelse; men hans instinkt drev ham fremad. Før officeren havde afsluttet sin sætning, red fyrst Andrej med ansigtet forvrænget af vrede hen til ham og løftede sin ridepisk.
»Vær... venlig... at lade — dem — passere!«
Officeren slog ud med armen og red hastigt bort.
»Det er hele skylden fra de folk på staben, at der er det her kaos,« mumlede han. »Gør som I vil.«

Fyrst Andrej red hurtigt bort fra lægekonen uden at løfte blikket — hun kaldte ham sin redningsmand — og idet han med afsky mindedes de mindste detaljer i denne ydmygende scene, galopperede han videre til den landsby, hvor han fik at vide, at den øverstkommanderende befandt sig.

Da han nåede landsbyen, steg han af hesten og gik hen til det nærmeste hus med den hensigt at hvile blot et øjeblik, spise noget og forsøge at ordne de sviende og pinefulde tanker, der forvirrede hans sind. »Det her er et pak af slyngler og ikke en hær,« tænkte han, idet han gik hen mod vinduet i det første hus, da en velkendt stemme kaldte ham ved navn.
Han vendte sig om. Nesvitskijs smukke ansigt kiggede ud fra det lille vindue. Nesvitskij, der bevægede sine fugtige læber, mens han tyggede på noget, og viftede med armen, kaldte ham indenfor.
»Bolkonskij! Bolkonskij!... Kan du ikke høre? Nå? Skynd dig herind!« råbte han.

Da fyrst Andrej trådte ind, så han Nesvitskij og en anden adjutant i gang med at spise. De vendte sig hurtigt mod ham og spurgte, om han havde nyheder. På deres velkendte ansigter læste han uro og ængstelse. Det var særligt tydeligt på Nesvitskijs normalt leende ansigt.
»Hvor er den øverstkommanderende?« spurgte Bolkonskij.
»Her, i det hus dér,« svarede adjutanten.
»Nå, er det sandt, at det er fred og kapitulation?« spurgte Nesvitskij.
»Det ville jeg spørge jer om. Jeg ved intet, bortset fra at jeg næsten ikke kunne komme hertil.«
»Og vi, min kære ven! Det er forfærdeligt! Jeg havde uret i at le ad Mack — det går os endnu værre,« sagde Nesvitskij. »Men sæt dig ned og spis noget.«
»De vil hverken kunne finde Deres bagage eller noget andet nu, fyrste. Og Gud ved, hvor Deres tjener Peter er,« sagde den anden adjutant.
»Hvor er hovedkvarteret?«
»Vi skal overnatte i Znaim.«

»Nå, jeg har fået alt det nødvendige pakket på to heste,« sagde Nesvitskij. »De har lavet glimrende pakker til mig — egnede til at krydse de bøhmiske bjerge med. Det ser sort ud, gamle ven! Men hvad er der med dig? Du må være syg, siden du ryster sådan,« tilføjede han og bemærkede, at fyrst Andrej var faret sammen som ved et elektrisk stød.
»Det er ingenting,« svarede fyrst Andrej.
Han var netop kommet i tanker om sit seneste møde med lægekonen og transportofficeren.
»Hvad laver den øverstkommanderende her?« spurgte han.
»Jeg kan slet ikke gennemskue det,« sagde Nesvitskij.
»Nå, det eneste, jeg kan gennemskue, er, at alting er rædselsfuldt, rædselsfuldt, ganske rædselsfuldt!« sagde fyrst Andrej og gik hen til det hus, hvor den øverstkommanderende opholdt sig.

Idet han passerede Kutuzovs (den øverstkommanderende) karet og de udmattede rideheste fra hans følge, med deres kosaksoldater, der talte højlydt sammen, trådte fyrst Andrej ind i gangen. Kutuzov selv, fik han at vide, var inde i huset med fyrst Bagration og Weyrother. Weyrother var den østrigske general, der havde efterfulgt Schmidt. I gangen sad den lille Kozlovskij på hug foran en skriver. Skriveren, der havde smøget manchetterne op, skrev hastigt på et omvendt badekar. Kozlovskijs ansigt så medtaget ud — han havde åbenbart heller ikke sovet hele natten. Han så på fyrst Andrej og nikkede ikke engang.
»Anden linje... har du skrevet det?« fortsatte han med at diktere til skriveren. »Kiev-grenadérerne, de podolske...«
»Man kan ikke skrive så hurtigt, Deres velbyrdighed,« sagde skriveren og så vredt og respektløst på Kozlovskij.

Gennem døren hørtes Kutuzovs stemme, ophidset og utilfreds, afbrudt af en anden, ukendt stemme. Af lyden af disse stemmer, den uopmærksomme måde Kozlovskij så på ham, den respektløse opførsel fra den udmattede skriver, den kendsgerning at skriveren og Kozlovskij sad på hug på gulvet ved et badekar så tæt på den øverstkommanderende, og fra den larmende latter fra kosakfolkene, der holdt hestene nær vinduet — af alt dette fornemmede fyrst Andrej, at noget vigtigt og skæbnesvangert var ved at ske.
Han henvendte sig til Kozlovskij med presserende spørgsmål.
»Om et øjeblik, fyrste,« sagde Kozlovskij. »Dispositioner for Bagration.«
»Hvad med kapitulationen?«
»Ikke tale om. Der er udstedt ordrer til kamp.«

Fyrst Andrej bevægede sig hen mod døren, hvorfra stemmerne lød. Netop som han skulle til at åbne den, ophørte lydene, døren åbnedes, og Kutuzov med sin ørnenæse og sit opsvulmede ansigt viste sig i døråbningen. Fyrst Andrej stod lige foran Kutuzov, men den øverstkommanderendes ene raske øje viste, at han var så optaget af tanker og bekymringer, at han slet ikke bemærkede hans tilstedeværelse. Han stirrede lige ind i sin adjutants ansigt uden at genkende ham.
»Nå, er du færdig?« sagde han til Kozlovskij.
»Et øjeblik, Deres excellence.«
Bagration, en mager midaldrende mand af middelhøjde med et fast, udtrykslyst ansigt af orientalsk type, trådte ud efter den øverstkommanderende.
»Jeg har den ære at præsentere mig,« gentog fyrst Andrej temmelig højt og rakte Kutuzov en konvolut.
»Ah, fra Wien? Udmærket. Senere, senere!«
Kutuzov gik ud på trappen med Bagration.
»Nå, farvel, fyrste,« sagde han til Bagration. »Guds velsignelse, og måtte Kristus være med dig i dit store forehavende!«

Hans ansigt blødgjordes pludselig, og tårer trådte ham i øjnene. Med venstre hånd trak han Bagration til sig, og med højre, hvorpå han bar en ring, gjorde han korsets tegn over ham med en bevægelse, der åbenbart var ham vane — han tilbød sin opsvulmede kind, men Bagration kyssede ham i stedet på halsen.
»Kristus være med dig!« gentog Kutuzov og gik hen mod sin karet. »Stig ind hos mig,« sagde han til Bolkonskij.
»Deres excellence, jeg ville gerne gøre nytte her. Tillad mig at forblive hos fyrst Bagrations deling.«
»Stig ind,« sagde Kutuzov, og da han bemærkede, at Bolkonskij stadig tøvede, tilføjede han: »Jeg har selv brug for gode officerer, selv brug for dem!«
De steg ind i kareten og kørte nogle minutter i tavshed.

»Der er stadig meget, meget foran os,« sagde han, som om han med en gammel mands skarpsindighed forstod alt, hvad der gik igennem Bolkonskijs tanker. »Hvis en tiendedel af hans deling vender tilbage, vil jeg takke Gud,« tilføjede han, som om han talte med sig selv.

Fyrst Andrej så på Kutuzovs ansigt, kun en fod fra sit eget, og lagde uvilkårligt mærke til de omhyggeligt vaskede ar nær hans tinding, hvor en kugle ved Ismail havde gennemboret hans kranium, og den tomme øjenhule. »Ja, han har ret til at tale så roligt om de mænds død,« tænkte Bolkonskij.
»Det er netop derfor, jeg beder om at blive sendt til den deling,« sagde han.

Kutuzov svarede ikke. Han syntes at have glemt, hvad han havde sagt, og sad hensunket i tanker. Fem minutter senere, sagte vuggende på karetens bløde fjedre, vendte han sig mod fyrst Andrej. Der var ikke spor af uro i hans ansigt. Med fin ironi stillede han fyrst Andrej spørgsmål om detaljerne i hans samtale med kejseren, om bemærkninger han havde hørt ved hoffet om Krems-affæren, og om nogle damer, de begge kendte.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: That same night, after taking leave of the Minister of War, Bolkónski set off to rejoin the army, not knowing where he would find it and fearing he might be captured by the French on the way to Krems.

In Brünn, everyone connected to the court was packing up, and the heavy baggage had already been dispatched to Olmütz. Near Hetzelsdorf, Prince Andrew reached the main road along which the Russian army was moving at great speed and in complete disorder. The road was so clogged with wagons that it was impossible to get through in a carriage. Prince Andrew got a horse and a Cossack escort from a Cossack commander, and hungry and exhausted, threading his way past the baggage wagons, he rode in search of the commander in chief and his own luggage. The most alarming reports about the army's situation reached him as he went, and the sight of the troops in their chaotic retreat confirmed every rumor.

He remembered words from Bonaparte's address to his army at the beginning of the campaign: [Speaking in French] "That Russian army which English gold has transported from the ends of the earth—we shall make it share the same fate as the army at Ulm." These words awakened in him astonishment at his hero's genius, a sting of wounded pride, and a hope for glory. "And if all that's left is to die?" he thought. "Well, if it comes to that, I'll do it no worse than anyone else."
"That Russian army which has been brought from the ends of the earth by English gold, we shall cause to share the same fate—the fate of the army at Ulm."

He looked with contempt at the endless, chaotic mass of detachments, wagons, guns, artillery pieces, and still more baggage trains and vehicles of every kind, overtaking one another and blocking the muddy road three and sometimes four abreast. From all sides, in front and behind, as far as the ear could reach, came the rattle of wheels, the creaking of carts and gun carriages, the tramp of horses, the crack of whips, shouts, cursing from soldiers and orderlies and officers urging their horses on. Along both sides of the road lay fallen horses—some skinned, some not—and broken-down carts beside which solitary soldiers sat waiting for something. Other soldiers, breaking away from their units in groups, headed off to the nearby villages or returned from them dragging sheep, chickens, hay, and bulging sacks. On every uphill and downhill stretch the crowds grew denser and the shouting more frantic. Soldiers, sinking knee-deep in mud, pushed the guns and wagons with their own hands. Whips cracked, hooves slipped, harness straps snapped, and lungs were strained with shouting. The officers directing the march rode back and forth between the wagons. Their voices were barely audible over the uproar, and you could see from their faces that they had given up any hope of restoring order.
"Here's our beloved Orthodox Russian army," thought Bolkónski, remembering Bilíbin's words.

Wanting to find out where the commander in chief was, he rode up to a convoy. Coming straight toward him was a strange one-horse vehicle, obviously cobbled together by soldiers from whatever materials they could find—something between a cart, a buggy, and a carriage. A soldier was driving it, and behind the leather hood sat a woman wrapped in shawls. Prince Andrew rode up and was about to ask a soldier for directions when he was interrupted by the desperate screaming of the woman in the vehicle. An officer in charge of the transport column was beating the soldier who drove the woman's cart for trying to push ahead of the others, and his whip was landing on the vehicle's canvas cover. The woman shrieked piercingly. Seeing Prince Andrew, she leaned out from behind the cover and, waving her thin arms from beneath a woolen shawl, cried:

"Aide-de-camp! Aide-de-camp! For God's sake... protect me! What will become of us? I'm the wife of the doctor of the Seventh Chasseurs... They won't let us through, we've been left behind and lost our people..."
"I'll flatten you like a pancake!" shouted the angry officer at the soldier. "Turn back with your woman!"
"Aide-de-camp! Help me! What is happening?" screamed the doctor's wife.
"Let this cart through. Can't you see it's a woman?" said Prince Andrew, riding up to the officer.
The officer glanced at him, and without answering turned back to the soldier. "I'll teach you to push ahead!... Back!"
"Let them through, I said!" repeated Prince Andrew, his lips pressed tight.

"And who are you?" shouted the officer, turning on him in a state of drunken rage. "Who are you? Are you in command here? Eh? I'm in command here, not you! Get back or I'll flatten you like a pancake!" he repeated. The expression clearly pleased him.
"That was a nice put-down for the little aide-de-camp," came a voice from behind.

Prince Andrew saw that the officer was in that state of blind, drunken fury when a man doesn't know what he's saying. He realized that defending the doctor's wife in her ramshackle cart might expose him to what he dreaded more than anything in the world—ridicule. But his instinct drove him forward. Before the officer could finish his sentence, Prince Andrew, his face twisted with fury, rode straight at him and raised his riding whip.
"Let—them—through!"
The officer flung his arm in the air and hastily rode away.
"It's all the fault of these headquarters people—they're the ones causing this chaos," he muttered. "Do what you want."

Prince Andrew, without looking up, rode quickly away from the doctor's wife, who was calling him her savior. Recalling every detail of the humiliating scene with disgust, he galloped on to the village where he'd been told the commander in chief was located.

Reaching the village, he dismounted and went to the nearest house, hoping to rest even for a moment, eat something, and try to sort out the painful, tormenting thoughts swirling in his mind. "This isn't an army—it's a mob of scoundrels," he thought as he approached the window of the first house, when a familiar voice called out his name.
He turned around. Nesvítski's handsome face was looking out of a small window. Nesvítski, chewing something and moving his moist lips, was waving his arm and calling him over.
"Bolkónski! Bolkónski! Can't you hear me? Come here, quickly!" he shouted.

Going inside, Prince Andrew found Nesvítski and another adjutant eating. They spun around to face him, asking if he had any news. On their familiar faces he read alarm and anxiety. This was especially striking on Nesvítski's face, which was usually so cheerful.
"Where is the commander in chief?" asked Bolkónski.
"Here, in that house," answered the adjutant.
"Well, is it true? Peace and surrender?" asked Nesvítski.
"I was going to ask you. I know nothing except that I barely managed to get here."
"And us, my dear fellow! It's terrible! I was wrong to laugh at Mack—we're getting it even worse," said Nesvítski. "But sit down and have something to eat."
"You won't be able to find your baggage or anything else now, Prince. And God only knows where your man Peter is," said the other adjutant.
"Where is headquarters?"
"We're spending the night in Znaim."

"Well, I've managed to pack everything I need onto two horses," said Nesvítski. "They made up excellent packs for me—good enough to cross the Bohemian mountains. Things look grim, old friend! But what's wrong with you? You must be sick—you're shivering like that," he added, noticing Prince Andrew flinch as if from an electric shock.
"It's nothing," replied Prince Andrew.
He had just recalled his encounter with the doctor's wife and the transport officer.
"What is the commander in chief doing here?" he asked.
"I can't make it out at all," said Nesvítski.
"Well, all I can make out is that everything is dreadful, completely dreadful," said Prince Andrew, and he went off to the house where the commander in chief was staying.

Passing Kutúzov's carriage and the exhausted saddle horses of his entourage, with their Cossacks talking loudly together, Prince Andrew entered the hallway. Kutúzov himself, he was told, was inside with Prince Bagratión and Weyrother—the Austrian general who had replaced Schmidt. In the corridor, little Kozlóvski was squatting on his heels in front of a clerk. The clerk, with his sleeves rolled up, was scribbling furiously on an overturned tub. Kozlóvski's face looked haggard—he clearly hadn't slept all night either. He glanced at Prince Andrew without so much as a nod.
"Second line... have you written it?" he went on dictating to the clerk. "The Kiev Grenadiers, Podolian..."
"Can't write that fast, Your Honor," said the clerk, looking up at Kozlóvski with irritation and disrespect.

Through the door came the sounds of Kutúzov's voice—agitated and unhappy—broken by another voice, one Prince Andrew didn't recognize. From the sound of these voices, from Kozlóvski's distracted expression, from the clerk's rudeness, from the fact that both Kozlóvski and the clerk were squatting on the floor by a tub so close to the commander in chief, and from the noisy laughter of the Cossacks holding the horses by the window—from all of this, Prince Andrew sensed that something critical and catastrophic was about to happen.
He turned to Kozlóvski with urgent questions.
"One moment, Prince," said Kozlóvski. "Orders for Bagratión."
"What about a surrender?"
"Nothing of the sort. Orders are being drawn up for a battle."

Prince Andrew moved toward the door where the voices were coming from. Just as he was about to open it, the voices fell silent, the door swung open, and Kutúzov appeared in the doorway with his eagle nose and puffy face. Prince Andrew stood directly in front of him, but the expression in the commander in chief's one good eye showed he was so consumed by thoughts and worries that he didn't even register who was standing there. He stared straight at his adjutant's face without recognizing him.
"Well, have you finished?" he said to Kozlóvski.
"One moment, Your Excellency."
Bagratión, a lean middle-aged man of medium height with a firm, impassive face of Eastern features, emerged behind the commander in chief.
"I have the honor to present myself," said Prince Andrew, louder this time, holding out an envelope to Kutúzov.
"Ah, from Vienna? Very good. Later, later!"
Kutúzov walked out to the porch with Bagratión.
"Well, goodbye, Prince," he said to Bagratión. "My blessing, and may Christ be with you in your great endeavor!"

His face suddenly softened and tears welled in his eyes. With his left hand he drew Bagratión toward him, and with his right—on which he wore a ring—he made the sign of the cross over him in what was clearly a habitual gesture, offering his puffy cheek. But Bagratión kissed him on the neck instead.
"Christ be with you!" Kutúzov repeated, and turned toward his carriage. "Get in with me," he said to Bolkónski.
"Your Excellency, I would like to be of use here. Allow me to stay with Prince Bagratión's detachment."
"Get in," said Kutúzov, and when he noticed Bolkónski still hesitating, he added: "I need good officers myself. Need them myself!"
They got into the carriage and drove in silence for a few minutes.

"There is still much, much ahead of us," he said with the penetrating insight of an old man who seemed to understand everything passing through Bolkónski's mind. "If even a tenth of his detachment comes back, I shall thank God," he added, as if speaking to himself.

Prince Andrew glanced at Kutúzov's face, only a foot away, and found his eyes drawn to the carefully washed seams of the scar near his temple where a bullet had pierced his skull at Ismail, and to the empty eye socket. "Yes, he has earned the right to speak so calmly about those men's deaths," thought Bolkónski.
"That is why I ask to be sent to that detachment," he said.

Kutúzov did not answer. He seemed to have forgotten what he'd been saying and sat sunk in thought. Five minutes later, swaying gently on the soft springs of the carriage, he turned to Prince Andrew. There was not a trace of emotion on his face. With subtle irony, he began questioning Prince Andrew about the details of his interview with the Emperor, about the remarks he'd heard at court regarding the Krems affair, and about certain ladies they both knew.
